summary: Defines terminology for benchmarking devices that forward IP multicast traffic. Common terms let test results be compared across different devices and labs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When people test machines that copy and send data to many receivers, they must use the same words so their numbers can be compared. This sets the words.

questions: how are multicast forwarding devices benchmarked
how to test multicast device performance
subtitle: Standard metrics for measuring how well network devices handle one-to-many traffic.

tldr.problem: When testing network devices that forward multicast traffic, different labs use different terms and measurement methods, making it hard to compare performance results or understand what claims mean.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a set of standard terms and metrics for multicast benchmarking, covering throughput, latency, overhead, group capacity, and interactions between different traffic types and operations.
tldr.outcome: Labs can now run comparable multicast tests using shared terminology, making it easier for network designers to choose devices and vendors to compare their performance fairly.

today: RFC 2432 is an Informational RFC that provides the terminology for the Benchmarking Methodology Working Group. It enabled the publication of methodology documents (like RFC 3918 for multicast benchmarking methodology) that detail how to collect these metrics correctly.

sections.title: Why Multicast Benchmarking Needs Standard Terms
sections.content:
Unicast (one-to-one) and multicast (one-to-many) traffic place different demands on network devices. A single multicast packet must be replicated and forwarded to multiple destination ports, which can use more processing resources or memory than a single unicast packet. Device architecture, shared memory design, protocol requirements, and the complexity of managing groups all affect performance.

RFC 1242 and RFC 2285 defined benchmarking terms for general network devices, but they focused on unicast and homogeneous traffic. RFC 2432 extends those efforts to the multicast domain, so that vendors, testers, and buyers can measure and discuss multicast performance consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: When a device sends mail to one person, it is pretty simple. When it sends to 100 people at once, things get complicated and slow. People testing these devices need the same words for what 'complicated and slow' means, so they can compare devices fairly.

sections.title: Throughput and Forwarding Metrics
sections.content:
Mixed Class Throughput (MCT) measures the maximum rate at which a device can forward a mix of both unicast and multicast frames without loss. This reflects real-world conditions, where devices must handle both types. Scaled Group Forwarding Matrix (SGFM) shows how forwarding rate changes as the number of multicast groups increases, testing scalability. Aggregated Multicast Throughput (AMT) measures the maximum rate when forwarding a single multicast group to N destination ports, showing how device performance depends on the number of output interfaces.

Encapsulation Throughput (ET), Decapsulation Throughput (DT), and Re-encapsulation Throughput (RET) measure performance when multicast packets must be tunneled or reformatted (for example, to traverse non-multicast network segments). These metrics help characterize the overhead of protocol conversion.
sections.plainLanguage: Different metrics answer different questions: 'How much mixed unicast and multicast can it handle?' 'What happens if I have 10 multicast groups? 100 groups?' 'How slow does it get if I have to wrap multicast packets in a tunnel?' Each metric is measured in packets per second.

sections.title: Delay and Group Management Metrics
sections.content:
Multicast Latency (ML) is the set of individual delays from an input port to each output port in a multicast group, letting testers understand whether the device treats all destinations equally or whether some paths are slower. Min/Max Multicast Latency is the difference between the slowest and fastest destination, which matters for synchronized applications (like networked games or multimedia).

Group Join Delay (GJD) measures how quickly a device starts forwarding multicast packets after receiving an IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) join request. Group Leave Delay (GLD) measures how quickly it stops forwarding after a leave request. These metrics matter because users may briefly receive no multicast traffic or stale traffic during transitions.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask a machine to join a group and get the show, how long before you see it? If you ask to leave, how long before it stops? And when the show goes to 100 people at once, does person #1 see it at the same time as person #100?

sections.title: Capacity and Group Limits
sections.content:
Multicast Group Capacity (MGC) is the maximum number of multicast groups a device can support while still forwarding frames to all groups correctly. Different devices handle large numbers of groups differently: some use hardware forwarding tables that fill up quickly, others use software lookups that slow down, and some manage group state in ways that impose limits.

The RFC notes that the relationship between the number of groups and the number of sources per group matters. Some multicast routing protocols track (source, group) pairs rather than just groups, which can make the forwarding table larger and the group capacity smaller. Frame size and forwarding table size also interact in complex ways.
sections.plainLanguage: A machine can probably handle 10 TV channels, maybe 100, maybe 1000. But at some point the machine's brain fills up and it cannot keep track of them all. This metric is 'how many channels can you really handle?'

sections.title: Performance Under Load and Interactions
sections.content:
A burdened response is a metric collected while the device is under another load or constraint. Forwarding Burdened Multicast Latency (FBML) measures multicast latency while the device is simultaneously forwarding a large amount of other traffic, showing how performance degrades under load. Forwarding Burdened Group Join Delay (FBGJD) measures join delay while traffic is already flowing.

The RFC cautions that burdened metrics are good for characterizing a single device but risky for comparing devices, because results depend heavily on configuration, timer settings, and test conditions. A well-configured test on one device might look great; a poorly configured test on another might look terrible, even if the devices are equally capable. Results must be reported together with the imposed load and forwarding rate, not in isolation.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask a machine to do ten things at once, it might get confused. These metrics measure 'what is the latency when we are already asking it to work hard?' The tricky part is: does the machine get confused because it is bad, or because we set it up wrong?
